{
"title": "The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries",
"authors": "Shahid Khalid, Nicolò Pianta, Simone Bonizzoni, Piercarlo Mustarelli, Riccardo Ruffo",
"field_subfield": "Electrochemistry / Materials for Energy Storage",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental study",
"executive_summary": "This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors motivate their research by highlighting the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on organic electrolytes with low flashpoints, high viscosities, and thermally unstable salts like LiPF6 that degrade in the presence of moisture. While aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety and environmental benefits, they suffer from a narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in diluted solutions. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored high-concentration regimes, culminating in the concept of water-in-salt electrolytes (WISE), where low water activity enables wider voltage windows. However, fluorinated salts commonly used in WISE systems are toxic, expensive, and scarce, prompting the search for cost-effective alternatives like acetate salts. The authors prepare four binary electrolytes with constant 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK and varying CH3COONa concentrations (1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹), along with a 1 M NaAc reference. They characterize the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of these solutions, finding that the most concentrated electrolyte (7N20K) offers the best compromise between conductivity (21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C) and electrochemical stability (up to 3 V). As a proof of concept, they demonstrate the use of this electrolyte with a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode, which reversibly inserts and de-inserts Na⁺ ions at about -0.7 V vs. SHE, achieving a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, 96% average charge efficiency at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The excellent interfacial kinetics are evidenced by a low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. These results support the feasibility of designing alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries using the water-in-salt approach with safe, abundant acetate-based electrolytes.",

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid, Nicolò Pianta, Simone Bonizzoni, Piercarlo Mustarelli, Riccardo Ruffo
summary.executive_summary: This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors motivate their research by highlighting the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on organic electrolytes with low flashpoints, high viscosities, and thermally unstable salts like LiPF6 that degrade in the presence of moisture. While aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety and environmental benefits, they suffer from a narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in diluted solutions. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored high-concentration regimes, culminating in the concept of water-in-salt electrolytes (WISE), where low water activity enables wider voltage windows. However, fluorinated salts commonly used in WISE systems are toxic, expensive, and scarce, prompting the search for cost-effective alternatives like acetate salts. The authors prepare four binary electrolytes with constant 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK and varying CH3COONa concentrations (1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹), along with a 1 M NaAc reference. They characterize the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of these solutions, finding that the most concentrated electrolyte (7N20K) offers the best compromise between conductivity (21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C) and electrochemical stability (up to 3 V). As a proof of concept, they demonstrate the use of this electrolyte with a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode, which reversibly inserts and de-inserts Na⁺ ions at about -0.7 V vs. SHE, achieving a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, 96% average charge efficiency at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The excellent interfacial kinetics are evidenced by a low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. These results support the feasibility of designing alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries using the water-in-salt approach with safe, abundant acetate-based electrolytes.

claims.description: Highly concentrated aqueous acetate electrolytes can support sodium-ion batteries with good performance.
The 7N20K electrolyte offers the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors motivate their research by highlighting the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on organic electrolytes with low flashpoints, high viscosities, and thermally unstable salts like LiPF6 that degrade in the presence of moisture. While aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety and environmental benefits, they suffer from a narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in diluted solutions. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored high-concentration regimes, culminating in the concept of water-in-salt electrolytes (WISE), where low water activity enables wider voltage windows. However, fluorinated salts commonly used in WISE systems are toxic, expensive, and scarce, prompting the search for cost-effective alternatives like acetate salts. The authors prepare four binary electrolytes with constant 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK and varying CH3COONa concentrations (1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹), along with a 1 M NaAc reference. They characterize the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of these solutions, finding that the most concentrated electrolyte (7N20K) offers the best compromise between conductivity (21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C) and electrochemical stability (up to 3 V). As a proof of concept, they demonstrate the use of this electrolyte with a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode, which reversibly inserts and de-inserts Na⁺ ions at about -0.7 V vs. SHE, achieving a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, 96% average charge efficiency at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The excellent interfacial kinetics are evidenced by a low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. These results support the feasibility of designing alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries using the water-in-salt approach with safe, abundant acetate-based electrolytes.

Research Context
Super-concentrated aqueous electrolytes are attracting interest for safer, cheaper batteries. Conventional lithium-ion batteries suffer from safety and cost issues. Organic electrolytes have low flashpoints and high viscosities. LiPF6 degrades in moisture, producing HF and corrosion. Aqueous electrolytes have a narrow water stability window of 1.23 V. Diluted aqueous systems can only reach about 1.5 V stability. Water-in-salt electrolytes enable wider voltage windows via low water activity. Fluorinated salts are toxic, expensive, and scarce. Acetate salts are cost-effective, soluble, and abundant alternatives. NASICON materials are ideal electrodes due to stable structure and large channels.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether acetate-based WISE electrolytes can support sodium-ion batteries. The authors hypothesize that increasing NaAc concentration improves electrochemical stability. They predict that 7N20K offers the best balance of transport and stability. They expect good conductivity despite high concentration. They anticipate wide stability window in ideal conditions. They predict reversible Na⁺ insertion in NASICON at about -0.7 V. They expect high charge efficiency and capacity retention. They hypothesize low charge-transfer activation energy for good kinetics.

Methodological Details
NaAc and KAc were purchased at 99% purity from Alfa Aesar. Milli-Q water with conductivity of 6.7 µS cm⁻¹ was used as solvent. Four binary electrolytes were prepared with constant 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc. The four electrolytes are 1N20K, 2.5N20K, 5N20K, and 7N20K. A 1 M NaAc solution was prepared for comparison. Electrolytes were stored and used at room conditions. Compositional parameters are listed in Table 1. CLTP was synthesized via one-pot sol-gel route. Ammonium dihydrogen phosphate was used as phosphate precursor. Titanium was sourced from titanium butoxide. Lithium acetate dihydrate was used as lithium source. Glucose was used as carbon source.

Procedures And Architectures
The mixture was stirred for 4 h at 55°C in a sealed container. The system was opened and heated to 80°C to remove ethanol. The precursor was dried under vacuum at 100°C. The powder was calcined at 800°C for 6 h under argon. The ramp rate was set to 5°C min⁻¹ with gas flow of 50 ml min⁻¹. Pristine LTP was synthesized via the same route without glucose. XRD was performed using Rigaku Miniflex 600 with Cu cathode. XRD analysis covered 2θ range from 10° to 80° with step size of 0.02. SEM was done using Zeiss Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity was measured with MCR Rheometer 102 using parallel plate. Shear rates ranged from 10 to 300 s⁻¹ at temperatures 10-40°C. DSC was performed using DSC 1Star with Mettler Toledo.

Key Results
Tg increases with salt concentration, indicating salt-in-water to water-in-salt transition. 1N20K and 2.5N20K did not show cold crystallization or melting endotherm. 5N20K and 7N20K showed cold crystallization at -28.06°C and -33.70°C. Melting endotherms were recorded for 5N20K and 7N20K around 0°C. All compositions follow Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher behavior. Ionic conductivity decreases with increasing concentration. 7N20K exhibits conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C. Viscosity increases with concentration, following Arrhenius behavior. Acetate salts behave as structure-making salts. All electrolytes behave like Newtonian fluids. All electrolytes are classified as quasi-ideal electrolytes. 7N20K follows Kohlrausch's law of strong electrolytes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Tg shift indicates growing interactions among solution species. Low liquidus temperature prevents premature cell failure. Conductivity decrease is related to Tg shift and increased viscosity. Strong ion-water interactions suggest formation of water-salt structures. Anions interact with cations without significant reassociation. Cathodic stability increase confirms hydrogen evolution suppression. Anodic ESW expansion is less significant than cathodic. Low charge-transfer activation energy proves good interfacial kinetics.

Contradictions And Limitations
The LSV procedure may overestimate decomposition limits. The procedure involves a large amount of electrolyte. The procedure uses a quasi-ideal electrocatalytic electrode with small surface area. The stability window is only achieved in ideal conditions. Ideal conditions require flooded cell and highly electrocatalytic electrode.

Claims
Highly concentrated aqueous acetate electrolytes can support sodium-ion batteries with good performance. The 7N20K electrolyte shows good conductivity. The 7N20K electrolyte shows wide stability window. The NASICON electrode reversibly inserts Na⁺ ions. The first cycle anodic capacity is 85 mAh g⁻¹. The average charge efficiency is 96% at low current. The capacity retention is 90% after 60 cycles. The stability window is only achieved in ideal conditions. The procedure may overestimate decomposition limits. The results support the feasibility of alkaline-ion batteries. The acetate electrolytes are safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly. The NASICON electrode is a promising anode material.
The 7N20K electrolyte offers the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability. The 7N20K electrolyte shows good conductivity. The 7N20K electrolyte shows wide stability window. The 7N20K electrolyte has low liquidus temperature. The stability window is only achieved in ideal conditions. The procedure may overestimate decomposition limits. The 7N20K electrolyte is suitable for sodium-ion batteries. The 7N20K electrolyte prevents premature cell failure.

Data And Code Availability
The supporting information is available free of charge. The supporting information includes shear stress vs shear rate curves. The supporting information includes XRPD patterns and SEM images. The supporting information includes additional electrochemical characterization.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The 1 M NaAc solution was used for comparison. The CLTP electrode was compared with pristine LTP. The CLTP electrode was tested in 7N20K and 1 M NaAc. The performance in WISE electrolyte is better than diluted solution.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is the development of acetate-based WISE electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The strongest evidence is the 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The future path is the development of alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries using water-in-salt approach.
